old: Its root once named a hollowed-out vessel carved for water travel in the Caribbean.
The word for it entered Spanish as "canoa" before crossing into English in the 1500s.
Its Proto-Arawak ancestor *kanawa also gave rise to Wayuu "anuwa" and Lokono "kanoa."
clues: This kind of small boat takes its name from Taíno, a language of the Caribbean, and the word spread into nearly every language that met it.
A narrow, open boat pointed at both ends and moved with single-bladed paddles, unlike a kayak with its covered deck. The Taíno original named a boat hollowed from a single log.
Someone fiercely self-reliant is said to paddle their own one of these, and a related word in the Arawakan language Lokono is kanoa, also meaning boat.
